title: Collective Quantum Logic Spectroscopy
authors: Raphael Kaubruegger, Matthew Patkowski, Yicheng Zhang, Robert J. Lewis-Swan, David B. Hume, Ana Maria Rey
abstract: Scaling trapped-ion quantum sensors from single ions to large ensembles is a key challenge for next-generation precision measurements. At the same time, many ion species of interest for optical clocks and tests of fundamental physics lack closed cycling transitions required for direct laser cooling and state detection. Collective quantum logic spectroscopy addresses both limitations by coupling an ensemble of sensor, or spectroscopy, ions to one or more logic ions that provide sympathetic cooling and state readout. Here, we establish the fundamental performance limits and operating regimes of this protocol, identifying how the interaction strength, interrogation time, and logic-ensemble size govern sensitivity, dynamic range, and robustness to experimental imperfections. We show that quantum-limited sensitivity can be retained even with a single logic ion, while increasing the number of logic ions substantially improves readout efficiency and robustness. Beyond precision metrology, the same collective interface enables many-body measurements relevant to quantum information processing, including parity measurements and stabilizer-like syndrome extraction. Our results establish collective quantum logic spectroscopy as a scalable framework for optical clocks, quantum-enhanced sensing, and trapped-ion quantum information processing.
summary: This paper introduces Collective Quantum Logic Spectroscopy (QLS) as a powerful, scalable technique for improving precision measurements in trapped-ion quantum sensors. By coupling a large ensemble of sensing ions to a smaller set of logic ions, it overcomes limitations in ion species and scaling. The theoretical analysis quantifies the performance limits, showing how the protocol can maintain quantum-limited sensitivity for applications ranging from optical clocks to quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of scaling trapped-ion quantum sensors to large ensembles while overcoming the limitation that many target ion species lack closed cycling transitions for direct laser cooling and state detection.
main_result: Collective Quantum Logic Spectroscopy (QLS) is established as a scalable framework that retains quantum-limited sensitivity even with a single logic ion, and whose performance can be tuned for both broad dynamic range and high precision.
method: The protocol involves coupling an ensemble of 'spectroscopy' ions to one or more 'logic' ions via a shared motional mode, implementing a sequence of controlled rotations and projective measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is a trapped-ion quantum sensor comprising an ensemble of spectroscopy ions (NS) coupled to logic ions (NL). The dynamics are modeled using collective spin operators and Hamiltonian terms describing spin-dependent displacements and mode interactions.
key_observables: Estimator variance ($\Delta^2_\phi$), sensitivity, dynamic range ($D_\phi$), and the collective rotation angle $	heta$.
important_parameters: Interaction strength, interrogation time, logic-ensemble size ($N_L$), and spectroscopy-ensemble size ($N_S$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Lamb-Dicke approximation, and the theoretical framework is agnostic to the specific implementation of the spin-dependent displacement.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the four-step protocol sequence involving logic and spectroscopy ions coupled to a shared motional mode. Figure 2 shows the dependence of the estimator variance on interaction strength ($	heta$) and spectroscopy imbalance ($\phi$).
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the QLS protocol, detailing the sequence of operations. It then quantifies the parameter estimation performance by analyzing the estimator variance in both small- and large-interaction regimes, concluding with a discussion on scaling laws and robustness against imperfections.
why_interesting: This work provides a comprehensive theoretical blueprint for enhancing quantum measurements in trapped ions by engineering collective interactions, which is central to quantum metrology and quantum information processing using atomic systems.
